paragraphs: This paper studies data poisoning as a way to discourage unauthorized learning from scraped data. The idea is to add changes that people barely notice but that interfere with model training. The authors identify a practical obstacle in existing approaches: generating those changes requires both the complete dataset and knowledge of the target model architecture.

Their proposed autoregressive poisoning method generates perturbations without access to the broader dataset. This changes the information needed to prepare a poisoned example: the creator does not need to assemble the collection into which it might later be scraped. The authors also describe the perturbations as generic, reporting that they work across different datasets and model architectures.

Compared with existing methods for making data unlearnable, the proposed poisons are reported to better withstand adversarial training and strong data augmentation. These findings suggest a more transferable and resistant poisoning approach, rather than guaranteed protection against every training procedure. The paper also analyzes the properties that make a poison effective.
neurips-2022-autoregressive-perturbation.tldr: Autoregressive perturbations poison training data without access to the broader dataset and show greater resistance to common defenses.

paragraphs: The paper addresses estimating an object's pose when the particular object was not seen during training but belongs to a familiar category. Existing category-level approaches remain limited to constrained environments, which the authors connect to the shortage of annotated data. Their goal is to extend this capability to more varied real-world instances and backgrounds.

The authors contribute Wild6D, a collection of unlabeled videos containing color and depth information, and a model called RePoNet. Training combines two sources of supervision: pose annotations available from synthetic data and an objective that matches silhouettes on real-world data. This lets the model learn from real examples without requiring 3D annotations for those training examples.

The method reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by a large margin on an existing dataset and the Wild6D test set. The latter has manual annotations specifically for evaluation. The distinction matters: the contribution reduces dependence on real-world 3D training labels while still checking pose predictions against annotated test examples.
neurips-2022-category-level-6d-object-po.tldr: RePoNet combines synthetic supervision with real-image silhouette matching to improve category-level pose estimation without real-world 3D training annotations.

paragraphs: Satellite image collections increasingly show places in fine detail across time, but finding meaningful events within those collections remains difficult. This paper focuses on changes that have a recognizable meaning, such as road construction. Its central problem is therefore discovering useful events within a large collection, rather than merely observing that images differ.

The authors introduce an unsupervised approach that searches a large collection of satellite images spanning locations and times for interesting changes. This avoids manually annotating the entire image corpus. Alongside the approach, they present datasets of change events and two benchmarks, CaiRoad and CalFire, covering road construction and forest fires.

These benchmarks support evaluating whether methods can retrieve or classify events according to their meaning. The authors examine several methods through both qualitative inspection and quantitative evaluation, finding that many existing approaches struggle with the datasets. The contribution supplies concrete evaluation problems for studying how systems move from detecting visual changes to recognizing the events those changes represent.
neurips-2022-change-event-dataset-for-di.tldr: The paper introduces unsupervised discovery of satellite-image change events and challenging benchmarks for road construction and forest fires.

paragraphs: An agent learning a new task may benefit from policies learned previously, but it must decide which policy is useful and when. Earlier reuse methods introduce additional learned components to make these choices. The authors argue that training those components can make optimization less stable or require substantial additional interaction with the environment.

CUP instead uses the critic already present in an actor-critic learning algorithm. At each state, it evaluates source policies and selects the one offering the greatest one-step improvement over the current target policy. These state-specific choices form a guidance policy. The target policy then learns with a regularization term that encourages it to imitate that guidance.

The paper provides a theoretical guarantee that the guidance policy monotonically improves on the current target policy. This guarantee concerns the constructed guidance policy, rather than asserting that every practical training update improves performance. Experiments report efficient transfer and substantial gains over baseline algorithms, supporting reuse of the existing critic as a useful policy-selection mechanism.
neurips-2022-cup-critic-guided-policy-re.tldr: CUP uses an agent's existing critic to select previously learned policies and guide efficient transfer without training extra components.

paragraphs: A robot may need to change its behavior when the environment's transition dynamics change. Context-aware meta-reinforcement learning addresses this by conditioning behavior on a compact description of the current dynamics. The difficulty studied here is that several underlying influences can change those dynamics together, making a useful context harder to infer from experience.

DOMINO learns a disentangled context, separating information about these influences within the representation. Its objective combines two goals: retaining information shared between the context and past trajectories, and reducing errors in predicting state transitions. The representation is therefore trained both to summarize relevant experience and to help explain how the environment changes from one state to the next.

The theoretical analysis shows that this decomposition can address underestimation of mutual information in the presence of multiple confounders and reduce sample requirements across environments. Experiments find benefits for both model-based and model-free reinforcement learning, including better sample efficiency and performance in unseen environments. The results support context decomposition as a useful route to adapting across changing dynamics.
neurips-2022-domino-decomposed-mutual-in.tldr: DOMINO learns disentangled context representations to help reinforcement-learning agents adapt more efficiently to changes in environment dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a deformable vision transformer can improve single-stage pedestrian detection while retaining fast inference. Its focus is the balance between detection accuracy and computational cost. The authors study transformer use across several common single-stage detector structures, rather than presenting performance improvements for only one architectural arrangement.

The proposed detector includes a module that enhances spatial features and features at multiple scales. The authors examine the architecture's design in depth and compare it with both single-stage and two-stage detectors. They report leading performance on Caltech and Citypersons while using fewer parameters than their baseline, connecting the accuracy improvements to a relatively compact model.

Reported log-average miss rates are 2.6% and 28.0% for the Reasonable and Heavy subsets of the Caltech test set, and 10.9% and 38.6% on the corresponding Citypersons validation subsets. On the Citypersons Heavy subset, the method also outperforms state-of-the-art two-stage detectors with considerably faster inference. These are results on the specified evaluations, supporting the proposed architecture's speed–accuracy balance.
neurips-2022-effectiveness-of-vision-tra.tldr: A deformable vision transformer with spatial and multi-scale feature enhancement delivers strong pedestrian detection results with fast inference.

paragraphs: The paper studies treatment decisions where the objective is to keep a physiological measurement within a safe interval and preferably near a desired level. The authors call this leveling. It differs from simply seeking the largest possible response: the desired outcome is proximity to a target, and patient characteristics affect which dose achieves it.

ESCADA is a multi-armed bandit algorithm designed around this objective. It makes personalized dose recommendations using contextual information while accounting for safety as it learns. The authors derive high-probability bounds on cumulative regret and provide safety guarantees. They also describe a related Thompson sampling method and explain why straightforward adaptations of algorithms such as GP-UCB may fit leveling poorly.

The evaluation uses computer simulations of bolus-insulin allocation for type-1 diabetes. Comparisons include GP-UCB, rule-based dose calculators, and a clinician. These simulations place the method in a concrete dosing problem; the abstract does not report a comparative winner. The contribution combines a target-seeking formulation, algorithms tailored to it, and theoretical analysis of performance and safety.
neurips-2022-escada-efficient-safety-and.tldr: ESCADA frames personalized dosing as safely learning to keep a physiological variable near a target and provides bandit algorithms with theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Preference models learn from comparisons, but predicting which option is preferred does not by itself explain that prediction. This paper addresses explanations for pairwise comparison data. Its aim is to make the reasoning represented by a preference model more understandable, including information that depends on the setting in which the comparison occurs.

The proposed framework, Pref-SHAP, builds on Shapley values. The authors derive value functions appropriate for preference models, giving the explanation framework a formulation tailored to comparisons. They then extend it to model and explain context-specific information. A tennis court's surface is the example given: the setting is part of what an explanation may need to account for.

The authors apply Pref-SHAP to synthetic and real-world datasets and report richer, more insightful explanations than the baseline. The stated contribution is explanatory rather than a claim of improved prediction accuracy. It connects a general approach to allocating explanatory credit with the particular structure of preferences and the contexts in which they are expressed.
neurips-2022-explaining-preferences-with.tldr: Pref-SHAP adapts Shapley-value explanations to pairwise preference models and context-specific information.

paragraphs: The paper examines predictive parity, a fairness requirement under which a positive prediction has the same probability of being correct across protected groups. It asks what the most accurate classifiers satisfying this requirement look like. This focuses on the reliability of positive predictions, a different fairness question from equalizing how frequently groups receive them.

The main theorem is conditional: when overall group performance levels differ only moderately, every fair Bayes-optimal classifier takes the form of group-specific threshold rules. When performance differs widely, that conclusion may fail. The authors also find that enforcing parity between groups can then produce unfairness within a group, revealing a tension that group-level measurements alone may obscure.

The proposed FairBayes-DPP algorithm adaptively selects thresholds, seeking predictive parity and high test accuracy when the stated condition holds. Experiments on synthetic and empirical data support the approach. The paper's contribution is both constructive and cautionary: it identifies a setting where thresholding has a theoretical foundation and a setting where that structure need not apply.
neurips-2022-fair-bayes-optimal-classifi.tldr: Under a condition on group performance differences, optimal predictive-parity classifiers use group-specific thresholds, motivating FairBayes-DPP.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds connect performance on observed data to performance beyond that data. Standard approaches based on empirical risk minimization depend heavily on the complexity of the available hypothesis class. This paper takes a different route by analyzing solutions obtained through distributionally robust optimization, which evaluates losses against a collection of plausible data distributions.

That collection is called an ambiguity set. The authors' bounds depend on its geometry and on how well it fits the true loss function. This shifts the central analytical question from the complexity of all candidate functions to the structure of distributional uncertainty and its relationship to the loss being studied.

For ambiguity sets defined through maximum mean discrepancy, Wasserstein distance, or phi-divergence, the analysis yields bounds depending on the true loss function without depending on other candidates in the hypothesis class. The authors describe this dependence as apparently minimal possible. The result offers a theoretical explanation of potential generalization benefits from robust optimization, without claiming that distributional uncertainty disappears.
neurips-2022-generalization-bounds-with-.tldr: The paper derives distributionally robust generalization bounds that depend on the true loss and ambiguity-set structure rather than other candidate hypotheses.

paragraphs: Category discovery becomes harder when unlabeled examples arrive continuously instead of being available together at the start. The system must recognize known categories while continuing to find new ones. The authors emphasize a representation conflict: features useful for distinguishing familiar classes may be less suitable for discovering categories that have not yet been identified.

Grow and Merge addresses this conflict by alternating between two phases. During growth, continuous self-supervised learning expands feature diversity to support discovery. During merging, the grown model is combined with a static model to maintain performance on known classes. These phases give discovery and familiar-category recognition distinct roles within the same ongoing learning process.

The authors report that extensive studies find this framework significantly more effective than state-of-the-art approaches for continuous category discovery. The finding supports deliberately balancing feature diversity with established classification ability as new data arrives. The contribution also makes the continuous setting explicit, drawing attention to a task that static category-discovery evaluations do not capture.
neurips-2022-grow-and-merge-a-unified-fr.tldr: Grow and Merge alternates feature expansion and model merging to discover new categories continuously while maintaining recognition of known ones.

paragraphs: Active learning requires deciding which arriving examples deserve a label request. This paper studies neural-network methods in a non-parametric streaming setting, where those decisions occur as data arrives. The authors introduce two regret measures based on population loss, aiming to assess learning performance more appropriately than the measure used in related state-of-the-art work.

Their algorithm uses neural representations both to exploit what has already been learned and to explore where more information is useful. Its label-query decision mechanism is designed for classification with multiple classes and comes with a performance guarantee. The design also uses full feedback and updates parameters in a manner the authors describe as more practical and efficient.

The resulting instance-dependent regret bound improves by roughly a logarithmic factor in T and removes the stated curse of input dimensionality. Under a hard-margin classification setting, the algorithm can eventually match the Bayes-optimal classifier. Experiments also report improved performance over leading baselines. The long-run optimality result specifically depends on the hard-margin condition.
neurips-2022-improved-algorithms-for-neu.tldr: The paper improves neural streaming active learning through new regret measures, a tailored query mechanism, and stronger conditional performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Causal discovery is complicated when recorded measurements are imperfect versions of the variables whose causal relationships matter. This paper studies recovering structure among those unobserved target variables. Its formulation assumes that the targets follow a linear, non-Gaussian model without causal cycles and that observations follow a random measurement-error model.

Existing methods for this formulation use over-complete independent component analysis, which the authors describe as difficult to scale. They propose the Transformed Independent Noise condition instead. It tests whether a particular linear transformation of some measured variables is independent of other measured variables. Non-Gaussianity and higher-order statistics make these tests informative about the underlying causal structure.

Using this condition, the authors establish identifiability of the causal model's ordered group decomposition. This is the specific structural result claimed, rather than unrestricted recovery of every causal detail. Independence tests can therefore recover a decomposition previously obtained through the more demanding analysis. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the method's effectiveness and reliability under the studied formulation.
neurips-2022-independence-testing-based-.tldr: Under linear non-Gaussian and measurement-error assumptions, transformed independence tests identify an ordered decomposition of hidden causal structure.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether integer arithmetic can support the entire training process for deep neural networks. The motivation is the growing computational burden of training and deployment, with lower-bit arithmetic offering potential savings in energy, memory, and latency. The question extends beyond computing predictions to back-propagation and stochastic gradient descent.

The authors propose changing the number representation used in computations directly, distinguishing their approach from recent quantization proposals. Their method forms a fully integer training pipeline. They report that it preserves the loss and accuracy trajectories of floating-point training without requiring special hyperparameter tuning, distribution adjustment, or gradient clipping.

Mathematical analysis and experiments lead the authors to conclude that integer arithmetic appears sufficient for training deep models. Evaluations cover classification, including vision transformers, object detection, and semantic segmentation. This breadth supports the method's applicability across several tasks. The stated conclusion remains qualified: the findings support integer training in the studied settings, rather than proving that every model and training procedure can be converted identically.
neurips-2022-is-integer-arithmetic-enoug.tldr: A fully integer training pipeline preserves reported floating-point learning trajectories across several tasks without special training adjustments.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a given sample contains enough information to determine the parameters of a deep ReLU network, at least locally. Local identifiability concerns distinguishing nearby parameter choices from their behavior on the sample. This is a question about what the observations determine, rather than whether a training algorithm can find those parameters.

The authors introduce a local parameterization that fixes some weights. They then construct lifting operators that represent the network through a smooth geometric space. In this representation, the network function combines a local lifting with a linear operator determined by the sample. Separating these pieces makes the sample's role in identifying parameters more accessible to geometric analysis.

The resulting theory gives a necessary and sufficient geometric condition for local identifiability. Analysis of tangent spaces further yields separate sharp, testable necessary and sufficient conditions. These conditions can be checked numerically through back-propagation and matrix-rank computations. The contribution connects an abstract uniqueness question with calculations that can test whether a particular sample supplies enough local information.
neurips-2022-local-identifiability-of-de.tldr: A geometric representation of deep ReLU networks yields numerically testable conditions for local parameter identifiability from a sample.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's three-dimensional body pose and movement could support home health monitoring, including remote rehabilitation training. Several sensor types can contribute, but the authors identify a shortage of datasets combining multiple sensing methods with this application focus. The paper introduces mRI to provide a shared resource for studying those combinations.

The dataset contains more than 160,000 synchronized frames from 20 people performing rehabilitation exercises. It brings together millimeter-wave radar, color and depth sensing, and wearable inertial sensors. Synchronization makes the different sensor records correspond in time, allowing research on the same activities through multiple modalities. The dataset supports benchmarks for both human pose estimation and action detection.

The authors conduct extensive experiments to characterize the strengths of individual modalities. The contribution is therefore both a collection of coordinated observations and an experimental examination of their usefulness. They present improved home health monitoring as a hoped-for application, while the demonstrated work supplies data and benchmarks for pose estimation, multimodal learning, and understanding actions.
neurips-2022-mri-multi-modal-3d-human-po.tldr: mRI provides synchronized radar, RGB-D, and inertial recordings of rehabilitation exercises for studying human pose and action detection.

paragraphs: Graph learning can struggle when supplied connections are incomplete, poorly suited to the task, or absent entirely. Learning new connections offers a possible remedy, but considering every pair of nodes normally creates a quadratic computational burden. NodeFormer addresses this tension between flexible communication and scalability when classifying nodes in large datasets.

The method introduces an all-pair message-passing scheme that allows signals to travel between arbitrary nodes. A kernelized Gumbel-Softmax operator enables differentiable learning of latent graph structure with complexity linear in the number of nodes. This makes potentially fully connected relationships available to the model without the usual quadratic scaling. The paper also supplies theory supporting this design.

Experiments report promising performance on node-classification tasks with graphs containing up to two million nodes. They also cover applications such as image classification where an input graph is missing. Together, these results support learning useful connectivity rather than relying entirely on a supplied graph, while making that approach computationally practical at the tested scales.
neurips-2022-nodeformer-a-scalable-graph.tldr: NodeFormer learns latent graph connections through all-pair message passing whose computational complexity scales linearly with node count.

paragraphs: Human judgments of an agent's behavior can depend on how events unfold over time. This paper extends reward modelling to account for such temporal dependencies. It removes an assumption attributed to existing work: that evaluators assess each step of a trajectory independently when providing feedback about the agent's behavior.

The authors formulate reward modelling as multiple instance learning. A complete trajectory is treated as a collection with an observed return label, while its individual steps have reward labels that are not observed. They develop models that capture time dependencies within these labeled trajectories. The approach connects an assessment of the whole sequence to the problem of learning rewards within it.

Across a range of reinforcement-learning tasks, the proposed models reconstruct reward functions with high reported accuracy and support training high-performing policies. These results indicate that trajectory-level labels can support learning temporally dependent rewards in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is broadening reward modelling to accommodate how earlier events can matter when interpreting later behavior.
neurips-2022-non-markovian-reward-modell.tldr: The paper learns temporally dependent rewards from whole-trajectory labels using multiple instance learning.

paragraphs: Predicting future user–item interactions requires representing both relationships among users and each user's changing interests. The authors argue that mixing these factors implicitly can create noisy representations when they diverge. They also identify back-propagation-based parameter learning as a costly obstacle to updating user preferences in real time.

FreeGEM separates these concerns in a parameter-free dynamic graph method. An online module approximately updates user and item embeddings, a monitor estimates approximation error, and an offline module recalibrates embeddings when that error crosses a threshold. Attribute information is incorporated to better represent users from underrepresented groups. A separate interaction-pattern component combines changing time decay with attention to capture short-term personal interests.

On two link-prediction tasks, the authors report that FreeGEM can exceed state-of-the-art accuracy while improving efficiency by more than 36 times. The architecture ties this result to incremental updates and selective recalibration rather than repeated parameter training. Its parameter-free description does not remove operational choices: the method explicitly includes an error threshold for triggering recalibration.
neurips-2022-parameter-free-dynamic-grap.tldr: FreeGEM combines monitored incremental graph embeddings with personal interaction patterns, reporting strong link prediction and over 36-fold greater efficiency.

paragraphs: Standard transfer learning starts a downstream model from weights learned on a source task. The authors argue that this initialization conveys relatively little of the source knowledge and does not directly express how that knowledge should influence the downstream optimization landscape. They propose transferring a richer description of what the source task has taught.

The method learns informative posterior distributions on the source task using supervised or self-supervised learning. These distributions provide the basis for priors on the downstream task, modifying its whole loss surface. Source knowledge consequently affects the downstream objective, including the locations and shapes of optima, rather than entering only through the initial weights.

The authors report significant performance improvements and more data-efficient learning across downstream classification and segmentation tasks. They describe the approach as modular and usable in place of standard pre-training strategies. The informative priors can also be saved for later reuse, much like pretrained weights. This makes the transferred artifact a reusable description of learned knowledge that continues to shape downstream training.
neurips-2022-pre-train-your-loss-easy-ba.tldr: Informative priors learned from a source task reshape downstream training objectives and improve reported transfer performance and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Language models can produce unwanted properties such as toxicity, repetition, or an undesired sentiment. Quark addresses these behaviors by fine-tuning with a reward function that scores the property of interest. The objective is to reduce unwanted behavior while keeping the resulting model close to the original language model.

Training repeats a three-part cycle. The current model generates text, the samples are divided into reward quantiles, and each group receives a corresponding reward token. The model then trains on those samples using a standard language-modelling loss conditioned on the tokens. A KL-divergence penalty discourages excessive departure from the original model during this process.

At generation time, a high-reward token steers the model toward text with less of the unwanted property. Experiments on toxicity, negative sentiment, and repetition report improvements over strong baselines and reinforcement-learning methods including PPO. The contribution is a reward-driven procedure built from standard language-modelling operations, with demonstrated behavioral reductions rather than a guarantee that unwanted outputs become impossible.
neurips-2022-quark-controllable-text-gen.tldr: Quark uses reward-group tokens and ordinary language-model training to reduce unwanted text properties while limiting deviation from the original model.

paragraphs: A model's uncertainty estimates need to remain useful when deployment data differs from its training data. The authors emphasize that even mild distribution shifts can make this difficult. They identify a mismatch between that practical concern and much existing uncertainty-quantification research, which evaluates models when training and test data follow the same distribution.

The proposed multi-domain temperature scaling method uses data from several domains to calibrate predictions. Its central idea is to use differences among those domains as information for improving robustness under distribution shift. Instead of calibrating entirely around one distribution, the method incorporates heterogeneity into the calibration model itself.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets find that the approach outperforms existing methods on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test sets. This supports the use of multiple domains for calibration without showing a tradeoff in the reported within-distribution evaluations. The contribution concerns the reliability of uncertainty estimates under the tested shifts; the abstract does not claim that calibration is guaranteed for every future distribution.
neurips-2022-robust-calibration-with-mul.tldr: Multi-domain temperature scaling uses differences among data domains to improve calibration on both familiar and shifted test distributions.

paragraphs: In a zero-sum game, a Nash-equilibrium strategy can be conservative against an opponent whose weaknesses could be exploited. Directly optimizing against an estimated opponent model introduces a different problem: mistakes in that estimate can leave the player vulnerable. This paper studies how to improve performance against such opponents while retaining control over that vulnerability.

Safe Exploitation Search is a real-time search framework that continuously interpolates between these strategy-refinement extremes. The authors provide a theoretical upper bound on exploitability and a lower bound on evaluation performance. These bounds make the safety–exploitation tradeoff explicit, rather than treating either pure equilibrium play or an unrestricted response to the opponent model as the only option.

SES also supports efficient online adaptation as the opponent model changes, whereas previous safe-exploitation methods require recomputation across the whole game. Experiments report substantially better performance than equilibrium baselines and previous algorithms while maintaining low exploitability. Here, safety means bounded strategic vulnerability within the game, alongside the ability to capitalize on an opponent's weaknesses.
neurips-2022-safe-opponent-exploitation-.tldr: Safe Exploitation Search adapts to opponent weaknesses through real-time refinement while providing bounds on exploitability and evaluation performance.

paragraphs: Image segmentation can be ambiguous because of noise or expert disagreement. Stochastic segmentation networks represent uncertainty, but an overall uncertainty prediction does not explain its individual components. This paper seeks to separate those components so that users can understand the variation and control which aspects change when sampling alternative segmentations.

The authors reinterpret the network head's low-rank Gaussian distribution over logits as a factor model. Its latent factors control individual uncertainty components. However, these factors are only identifiable up to orthogonal rotations, so their interpretation is not unique. The method uses rotations to encourage simpler, less redundant, and more separated components.

The paper introduces flow probabilities to quantify departures from the mean prediction, both overall and for individual factors. These quantities support visualization and help select rotations. Experiments on medical images, earth observation, and traffic scenes find that rotation criteria based on factor-specific flow probabilities consistently produce the best factors for fine-grained sampling. The contribution makes predicted uncertainty more structured and controllable, rather than merely reporting its magnitude.
neurips-2022-structuring-uncertainty-for.tldr: A factor-model interpretation separates segmentation uncertainty into components that can be rotated, visualized, and controlled during sampling.

paragraphs: Knowing which inputs matter to a nonlinear prediction model requires more than a single importance score when the learned function itself is uncertain. This paper develops a common framework for estimating variable importance while carrying that uncertainty into the result. It is designed to work across model families, including neural networks, kernel methods, and tree ensembles.

The importance measure is the squared partial derivative of the prediction function, integrated over the input distribution. In plain language, it summarizes how sensitive predictions are to changes in a particular input. The authors derive a posterior distribution for this importance quantity, so the output expresses uncertainty about importance rather than treating the learned prediction function as fixed.

The approach extends to models that are not differentiable, including tree ensembles. Bayesian nonparametric theory provides guarantees concerning posterior consistency and asymptotic uncertainty. Simulations and healthcare benchmark experiments report better variable selection than classical and recent alternatives. The contribution brings a shared sensitivity-based definition and uncertainty analysis to otherwise different nonlinear modelling approaches.
neurips-2022-towards-a-unified-framework.tldr: The paper estimates nonlinear variable importance with posterior uncertainty and theoretical guarantees across several model families.
